Q: Concurrent cache using SoftReferences behaves unpredictably under memory pressure, how to fix? A:
  • Sometimes objects disappear from the cache unexpectedly, even when memory usage is low.

This is what the API docs say about when soft references are cleared:

All soft references to softly-reachable objects are guaranteed to have been cleared before the virtual machine throws an OutOfMemoryError. Otherwise no constraints are placed upon the time at which a soft reference will be cleared or the order in which a set of such references to different objects will be cleared. Virtual machine implementations are, however, encouraged to bias against clearing recently-created or recently-used soft references.

(Emphasis added.)

It is therefore unclear what basis you have for expectations about when soft references to softly reachable objects in your cache will be cleared. Certainly the docs do not require memory pressure for clearance of soft references to softly reachable objects, and neither does the Oracle / OpenJDK implementation.

  • Occasionally, cleanup() causes high CPU usage under heavy load.

It should not be surprising that iterating through a large map is expensive. Especially so a concurrent map with contended access, and even more so if many modifications are made along the way.

Iterating the whole map is not at all what you should be doing here. If you register your SoftReferences with a reference queue then you can discover exactly which ones to remove from the cache by obtaining them from that queue. And if you subclass SoftReference then you can endow yours with references to the corresponding cache keys, so that you know which entries to remove without searching at all.

You could optionally avoid having an explicit cleanup() method at all by establishing a thread devoted to retrieving references to the queue as they become available and removing them immediately.

  • I’m not sure this is thread-safe when cleanup() runs concurrently with get() and put().

ConcurrentHashMap is thread safe in the sense that no data races arise from multiple threads performing operations on the same instance concurrently. Individual actions by one thread have their documented behavior regardless of actions by other threads. However, sequences of actions on a ConcurrentHashMap by one thread can suffer from interference from intervening actions by other threads unless some additional mechanism is employed to prevent it. This is not different from a Hashtable or a synchronized Map provided by Collections.synchronizedMap().

In your case, nothing in the specs for ConcurrentHashMap guarantees that the state of the map observed by your entry.getValue().get() is the same state affected by the subsequent it.remove(). Suppose, then, that a thread retrieves a SoftReference from the cache, observes it to have been cleared, and therefore constructs and caches a new a new one. It is possible that in the meantime, a thread running cleanup() also notices the cleared reference and therefore moves to drop it from the cache, but instead ends up removing the newly cached one. A similar sequence of events could result in distinct objects for the same key being live at the same time.

These are not necessarily failure cases for you per se, so maybe you don't want to account them thread safety issues, but they could certainly make your cache less effective.

  • Are there any concurrency issues with this implementation, especially with hundreds of threads?

See above. But also, hundreds of concurrently running platform threads could be its own concurrency issue. Context switching is expensive.

  • How do SoftReferences interact with GC under different memory pressures? Why might cached objects disappear unexpectedly?

Under sufficient memory pressure, SoftReferences to softly-reachable objects may be cleared sooner than they otherwise would be. On the flip side, lack of memory pressure is not a good reason to think that soft references will go uncleared indefinitely.

Q: How to sync a Python List of Canvas IDs with canvas.delete("all") to avoid errors in an Undo function? A:

This is a demo for using Redo and Undo in a tk.Canvas. I have replaced buttons with the conventional 'ctrl-z' = undo, 'ctrl-Z' = redo, also 'ctrl-Delete' to clear image and history.

The code operates by using two lists, one for redo and the other for undo. When drawing a line the data point is stored in the undo list, pressing 'ctrl-z' will pop it from undo list and append it to the redo list. The opposite happens when redoing the drawing. Key 'ctrl-Delete' will create a new canvas and history, creating a fresh start.

I've used your drawing method but tk.Canvas has both line and polygon objects as well as text, rectangle, oval and image. All could be controlled using this example.

import tkinter as tk
import random

root = tk.Tk()

class nmemonic:
    history = False
    last_x = last_y = 0

    def color(self):
        return random.choice(["red", "blue", "green", "black"])

    def make_history(self):
        self.history = True
        self.redoList = []
        self.undoList = []

the = nmemonic()

def update_coords(event):
    the.last_x, the.last_y = event.x, event.y

def draw_line(event):
    the.line_id = the.canvas.create_line(
        the.last_x, the.last_y, event.x, event.y, fill=the.color(), width=2)
    the.undoList.append(the.line_id)
    update_coords(event)

def undo(event):
    if len(the.undoList) > 0:
        the.last_item = the.undoList.pop(~0)
        the.redoList.append(the.last_item)
        the.canvas.itemconfig(the.last_item, state = "hidden")

def redo(event):
    if len(the.redoList) > 0:
        the.last_item = the.redoList.pop(~0)
        the.undoList.append(the.last_item)
        the.canvas.itemconfig(the.last_item, state = "normal")

def makecanvas(event = None):
    # erase previous &| create as new
    the.make_history() 

    the.canvas = tk.Canvas(root, takefocus = 1, width=400, height=300, bg="white")
    the.canvas.grid(row=0, column = 0, sticky = tk.NSEW)

    root.rowconfigure(0, weight = 1)
    root.columnconfigure(0, weight=1)

    the.canvas.bind("<Button-1>", update_coords)
    the.canvas.bind("<B1-Motion>", draw_line)
    the.canvas.bind("<Control-z>", undo)
    the.canvas.bind("<Control-Z>", redo)
    the.canvas.bind("<Control-KeyRelease-Delete>", clear_all)

    the.info = the.canvas.grid_info()
    the.canvas.focus_force()

def clear_all(event=None):
    the.canvas.destroy()
    makecanvas()
    
makecanvas()
root.mainloop()

Q: How can I parse a YAML file from a Linux shell script? A:

Update (2026): A Rust rewrite is now available as shyaml-rs — same CLI, no Python needed. much faster (x40), modern YAML 1.2 parser, and now support simple YAML edition.

I've written shyaml in python for YAML query needs from the shell command line.

Overview:

$ pip install shyaml      ## installation

Example's YAML file (with complex features):

$ cat <<EOF > test.yaml
name: "MyName !!"
subvalue:
    how-much: 1.1
    things:
        - first
        - second
        - third
    other-things: [a, b, c]
    maintainer: "Valentin Lab"
    description: |
        Multiline description:
        Line 1
        Line 2
EOF

Basic query:

$ cat test.yaml | shyaml get-value subvalue.maintainer
Valentin Lab

More complex looping query on complex values:

$ cat test.yaml | shyaml values-0 | \
  while read -r -d $'\0' value; do
      echo "RECEIVED: '$value'"
  done
RECEIVED: '1.1'
RECEIVED: '- first
- second
- third'
RECEIVED: '2'
RECEIVED: 'Valentin Lab'
RECEIVED: 'Multiline description:
Line 1
Line 2'

A few key points:

  • all YAML types and syntax oddities are correctly handled, as multiline, quoted strings, inline sequences...
  • \0 padded output is available for solid multiline entry manipulation.
  • simple dotted notation to select sub-values (ie: subvalue.maintainer is a valid key).
  • access by index is provided to sequences (ie: subvalue.things.-1 is the last element of the subvalue.things sequence.)
  • access to all sequence/structs elements in one go for use in bash loops.
  • you can output whole subpart of a YAML file as ... YAML, which blend well for further manipulations with shyaml.

More sample and documentation are available on the shyaml github page or the shyaml PyPI page.

Q: WidgetKit: Image from Assets.xcassets fails to load (errno = 2), but direct file access works A:
  1. Select your Widget Extension target (not the main app target)
  2. Go to Build Phases → Copy Bundle Resources
  3. is your Assets.xcassets listed there?

Q: Converting object column in pandas dataframe to datetime A:

It means you have an extra space. Though pd.to_datetime is very good at parsing dates normally without any format specified, when you actually specify a format, it has to match EXACTLY.

You can likely solve your issue by adding .str.strip() to remove the extra whitespace before converting.

import pandas as pd
df['Time stamp'] = pd.to_datetime(df['Time stamp'].str.strip(), format='%d/%m/%Y')

Alternatively, you can take advantage of its ability to parse various formats of dates by using the dayfirst=True argument

df['Time stamp'] = pd.to_datetime(df['Time stamp'], dayfirst=True)

Example:

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'Time stamp': ['01/02/1988', '01/02/1988 ']})

pd.to_datetime(df['Time stamp'], format= '%d/%m/%Y')

ValueError: unconverted data remains:

pd.to_datetime(df['Time stamp'].str.strip(), format='%d/%m/%Y')
#0   1988-02-01
#1   1988-02-01
#Name: Time stamp, dtype: datetime64[ns]

pd.to_datetime(df['Time stamp'], dayfirst=True)
#0   1988-02-01
#1   1988-02-01
#Name: Time stamp, dtype: datetime64[ns]

Q: Storing numbers as varchar A:

You can store leading zeroes to a varchar that you can't do with integer columns (eg. it is possible to have difference between 123 and 0000123). For example zip codes in some countries. However, if you need to do that, then you are really dealing with textual information that should have varchar column. For example, phone numbers or zip codes should definitely go to a varchar column.

Otherwise if you are using your data like numbers (adding them together, comparing them, etc.) then you should put it into integer column. They consume far less space and are faster to use.
